Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 104, verse 1–9:

﴿Woe to every slanderer and backbiter.﴾ He is, in general, one who disparages people and devours their honour. It is derived from al-hamz (defamation to the face) and al-lamz (defamation behind the back), and the pattern fu'alah (ḥumazah, lumazah) is used for intensification. Scholars differed over the difference between the two words. It was said: al-hamz is in presence and al-lamz is in absence; it was also said: the reverse. It was said: al-hamz is by hand and eye, and al-lamz is by tongue; and it was said: the two are the same. The surah was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, because he was much given to slandering people. It was also said: concerning Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and it was said: concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. Nevertheless, its wording is general, applying to everyone who possesses these qualities. ﴿And who amasses wealth and counts it﴾: that is, he counts it and keeps account of its number, lest it decrease, and so he withholds it from good deeds. It was also said: the meaning is that he prepares it and stores it as a reserve against the calamities of time. ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾: that is, he supposes, out of extreme ignorance and deception, that his wealth will make him abide in the world. It was also said: he supposes that his wealth will bring him to the abode of eternity. ﴿No! He will surely be thrown into al-Ḥuṭamah﴾: a rebuttal of what he supposed. This is the answer to an omitted oath. Al-Ḥuṭamah is Hell, and it was named Ḥuṭamah because it crushes whatever is cast into it and burns it fiercely. He magnified it by saying: ﴿And what will make you know what al-Ḥuṭamah is?﴾ Then he explained it: ﴿It is the Fire of Allah, kindled, which rises over the hearts﴾: that is, it reaches the hearts with its burning. Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: it may mean that it looks upon what is in the hearts of beliefs and intentions, by Allah's making it aware of them. ﴿Closed over them﴾: sealed shut. ﴿In extended columns﴾: al-'umud is the plural of 'amud (column), and according to Sibawayh it is a collective noun; it is also read as 'umud with two dammas. The 'amud is a long piece of iron or wood, and al-mumaddadah means extended, long. There are two opinions regarding the meaning. The first: the gates of Hell are closed upon them, and then columns are extended across its gates to strengthen the locking and bolting, just as house doors are secured with columns; on this view the prepositional phrase is connected to muṣadah (closed). The second: they are bound and shackled within the columns, so the prepositional phrase in this case occupies the position of the predicate of an implied subject, its estimated sense being: they are bound in columns.
